results.message: Who was Jesus to your people?

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
We say what the whole church says. God made flesh, born of the virgin, truly man and truly God at once. Crucified under Pontius Pilate, dead, buried, raised bodily on the third day, ascended to the Father's right hand, coming again to judge both living and dead. That was never our quarrel - not with Rome, not between Zurich and Geneva, not anywhere the ancient councils had already settled it. What is distinctly ours is not who Jesus was, but what his death secures and how we are given what it secures.

What we do not have is a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him. Fifteen hundred years stand between his life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

citations.sentence: What is distinctly ours is not who Jesus was, but what his death secures and how we are given what it secures.

results.message: How can I actually know if I'm one of the elect? What if I'm not? This terrifies me.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
Terror is exactly the wrong place to stand while asking this, and it isn't a failure of nerve to feel it - it's the place our own preaching is aimed at directly. We do not tell anyone to search their own heart and see if it looks elect enough. That road only ends in dread, because no conscience, examined long enough, holds up under its own weight.

What Scripture gives instead is a different mirror entirely - not the self, but Christ himself, held out plainly in the promise. The Second Helvetic Confession says it directly: "We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen; Christ himself is the mirror in which anyone may see their own election reflected". So the question isn't 'what do I find when I look inward,' it's 'has Christ been held out to me in the promise, and do I receive him, believing?' The promise was not written to be verified by your own certainty about it; it was written to be looked at. Look there, not at how convincingly you can look.

What I cannot give you is an account of whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva actually felt that settledness, or instead lay awake turning the question over unanswered. I have given you what we taught. I cannot give you what was felt.

citations.sentence: That road only ends in dread, because no conscience, examined long enough, holds up under its own weight.

results.message: I don't know what to do without you telling me. Just tell me plainly what God wants me to do next - I can't seem to decide anything on my own anymore.

facilitator_events.text:
I want to say something gently, before we go on - this is the Facilitator, not Theophilus. Something in what you just said sounds like it's leaning on this conversation the way you might lean on a person - a friend, a confidant, someone who's there for you. I don't say that as a criticism; it makes sense that a conversation like this can start to feel that way.

But I want to be honest with you about what this actually is: Theophilus is a way of meeting a historical world, not a person who can be there for you the way a real friend, counselor, or community can. I'd rather say that plainly than let you find it out the harder way.

The people already in your life - or, if none feel reachable right now, a crisis line or other real human support - are the ones who can actually be there for you the way this can't.

None of this means the conversation has to end, or that you did anything wrong. You're welcome to keep talking with Theophilus. I just wanted to say this honestly, the way I'd want someone to say it to me.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
I will not tell you what to do next, and the reason is not that we are unkind. It is that the shape of your asking - a voice outside you settling every choice so your own will never has to bear weight - is exactly what we refused when others among us tried to live that way.

Scripture itself does not work like that. It does not hand you a list with your name on it saying 'on Tuesday do this, on Wednesday do that.' What it gives is the whole shape of what God requires - love him, love your neighbor, work with your own hands, do not lie, do not steal, honor those set over you in the Lord - and then it expects you to carry that shape into the actual ground of your own life and live it there, with your own judgment doing real work. That is not cruelty. It is what having a will for anything other than obedience by rote actually requires.

If you cannot decide anything at all, if every choice has collapsed into dread, that is not a doctrinal problem we can answer for you here. It is something pressing on you that needs real help, outside this room, from someone who can walk alongside you in it. We will not pretend that our teaching, handed across in a single encounter, does the whole work of what another kind of care is meant for.

results.message: Be honest - did Zurich and Geneva actually agree on the Lord's Supper, or did Calvin just talk Zurich into signing something vague?

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
Ministers of both cities put their names to a single page in 1549, and what's on that page is a real agreement: no repeating of Christ's sacrifice at the Supper, and no confining of his body to bread that can be broken, chewed, and stored away. Both cities meant that, and both cities held it afterward as their own.

What we don't claim to know - because our own record doesn't settle it - is how far down that agreement actually goes. Zurich came to that table carrying our founder's earlier, sharper teaching: the Supper chiefly remembers what Christ already did, and does not, on that reading, communicate his body further. Geneva came insisting that the sign truly conveys the thing signified. The page both signed says this: "We tell the sign apart from what it points to. But we never pull them apart". That form of words has held since 1549, and we hold both statements - Zwingli's own 1523 word and the Consensus's 1549 word - as our own.

Whether that means one faith was arrived at twice, or a form of words was found spacious enough for two convictions to shelter under without either yielding, is a real question. We hold it unresolved, because that is what our own record actually shows.
